title: A Falling Path That Never Repeats a Column

concept.title: To avoid one column, you only need the two smallest values of the previous row
body: Choose **one number from every row** of a table so that numbers from two **neighbouring rows are never in the same column**. What is the smallest possible total? For the table `1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9` the best choice is 1 + 5 + 7 = 13. (Unlike the earlier falling path, the next column can be any column except the previous one, not only the nearest.)

Let `best(i, j)` be the smallest total of a valid choice in the rows `0 .. i` that picks the cell `(i, j)`. It is `value(i, j)` plus the smallest `best(i - 1, c)` over all columns `c != j`. Searching the whole previous row costs O(w) per cell, O(h * w^2) in total. But the smallest value **excluding** one column is always either the overall smallest value of the row (if it is not in the excluded column) or the **second smallest** (if it is). So for each row remember only its two smallest values and where the smallest one is.

body.code:
prev = row0[:]
for row in rows[1:]:
    m1 = min(prev); i1 = prev.index(m1)               # the smallest value and its column
    m2 = min(v for c, v in enumerate(prev) if c != i1)   # the smallest value in the other columns
    prev = [row[j] + (m2 if j == i1 else m1) for j in range(w)]
print(min(prev))

body: This turns O(h * w^2) into O(h * w): 160 000 steps for a table of 400 by 400, against 64 million for the plain version. Whenever a DP asks for "the best of all except one", keep the best two (with the index of the best). A table with a single column and more than one row has no valid choice, which the limits exclude (`w >= 2`).

statement: A table with `h` rows and `w` columns is given. Choose exactly one number in every row so that the numbers chosen in two consecutive rows are in different columns. Print the smallest possible sum of the chosen numbers.
inputFormat: The first line has `h` and `w`: the number of rows and columns.
Each of the next `h` lines has `w` numbers.
hints: best(i, j) = value(i, j) + the smallest best(i - 1, c) over the columns c other than j.
The smallest value excluding one column is the overall smallest, or the second smallest if the overall smallest is in that column.
Keep the two smallest values of the previous row and the column of the smallest.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w = map(int, input().split())
a = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(h)]

# Your code here

explanation: best(i, j) is the value of the cell plus the smallest total of the previous row in another column; since that is the overall smallest total unless it lies in the same column (then the second smallest), only the two smallest totals and the column of the smallest are kept for every row. The answer is the smallest total of the last row.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w = map(int, input().split())
a = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(h)]

prev = a[0][:]
for i in range(1, h):
    m1 = min(prev)
    i1 = prev.index(m1)
    m2 = min(prev[:i1] + prev[i1 + 1:])
    row = a[i]
    prev = [row[j] + (m2 if j == i1 else m1) for j in range(w)]
print(min(prev))
